title: Reviewing school policies annually, and why it matters
description: A practical guide for Kenyan school principals and BOMs on reviewing school policies each year so they stay current, workable, and defensible.
body:
Policies are written once and then forgotten, until a dispute arrives and someone discovers the policy is out of date or says something nobody follows. A yearly review is a modest exercise that prevents that, and the end of the year is a natural time to do it.

A policy that is current, short, and known by everyone is far more useful than a long document in a cupboard.

Why policies go stale

The environment around schools keeps changing: CBE requirements, data protection rules, safeguarding expectations, and digital tools like WhatsApp and phones. A discipline policy written for the old curriculum, or an ICT policy that never mentioned smartphones, will not help when a real situation arises.

The core set most schools need

  • Discipline and student behaviour
  • Child protection and safeguarding
  • Admissions and transfers
  • Fees, payment plans, and bursaries
  • Health, safety, and emergency response
  • ICT, phones, and social media
  • Complaints and grievances
  • Data protection and privacy

Policies are evidence: During an audit, an inspection, or a dispute, a dated, approved, and regularly reviewed policy shows the school was acting responsibly. An undated one, or one nobody remembers, does not.

A simple review process

Ask a BOM committee or senior staff group to take the policies in turn, noting what is out of date, what is not followed in practice, and what is missing. Invite input from teachers, and where relevant, from student leaders and parents. Record the date of review, the changes made, and who approved them.

Share what changes

A policy only works if people know it. Give staff a short summary of changes, and give parents and students a plain-language one-page version of the policies that affect them most. Include the key rules in the induction for new staff and new learners.

Keep records that back up your policies.
